paras: The lynching of Gus Knight was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Bartow, Jefferson County, Georgia, on September 11, 1882. Knight, accused of assaulting a married white woman that morning, was taken from two constables and shot. Georgia papers presented the killing as deserved vengeance, and a short wire telegram carried it to papers across the South and Midwest.

Knight, described as a "mulatto" living on Judge Tarver's plantation, was accused of attacking a young married woman at her home about four miles south of Bartow around ten o'clock on the morning of Monday, September 11. According to the Louisville News and Farmer, he called her to the gate while her husband was away, chased her when she ran with her child in her arms, and then went to work at Donovan & Perkins' mill nearby. A later telegram identified her as the wife of Harmon McDaniel, "a respected farmer of Jefferson County."

The Bartow dispatch said Knight was captured, identified and confessed at a preliminary hearing. That night "the two constables on guard were overpowered by a mob," and Knight "was taken off and summarily disposed of." The Louisville paper gave a different sequence, in which a party of citizens found him at the mill about five in the evening, he confessed, and he was carried out before "the report of a number of guns was heard." The wire version said he was "riddled with bullets by a party of disguised men."
No report of an inquest, arrests of the men who killed Knight, or any official response appears in the coverage.

The Savannah Morning News ran the Bartow dispatch under the headline "SPEEDY VENGEANCE.! A Negro Fiend Lynched in Thomas County," calling Knight "the brute." Three days later it reprinted the Louisville News and Farmer, which called the killers "justly infuriated citizens" and remarked that Knight was unlikely to "appear again in his usual avocation and walks of life." Neither Georgia account named any member of the mob.

Outside Georgia the story traveled as a single sentence in columns of condensed telegrams, printed among accidents and other crimes in Tennessee, Mississippi and Missouri papers from late September to mid-October. A separate news roundup in Kentucky and Ohio weeklies mentioned only "a negro at Bartow" hanged by a mob, without his name.

The Savannah headline placed the lynching in Thomas County, while its own Bartow dateline, the Louisville paper and the wire telegram all placed it in Jefferson County. The Ohio and Kentucky roundup said the Bartow man was hanged on the same day as legal hangings on September 15, whereas the Georgia accounts and the wire describe a shooting on the night of September 11.

accounts.gist: Knight was captured, identified and confessed at a preliminary hearing; at night a mob overpowered the two constables guarding him and he was 'summarily disposed of.'

accounts.label: Louisville News and Farmer (local)
accounts.gist: Citizens found Knight at Donovan & Perkins' mill about five in the evening; he confessed, was carried out, and 'the report of a number of guns was heard.' No constables or hearing are mentioned.

accounts.label: Wire telegram
accounts.gist: Knight was arrested soon after, confessed, and was 'riddled with bullets by a party of disguised men.'

accounts.label: Weekly news summary
accounts.gist: A negro at Bartow, Ga., was 'hanged by mobs' on the same day as legal hangings on the 15th.

framing.detail: The Savannah Morning News headed it 'SPEEDY VENGEANCE.! A Negro Fiend Lynched' and called Knight 'the brute'.
The Louisville News and Farmer called the mob 'justly infuriated citizens' and joked that Knight would not 'appear again in his usual avocation'.
Papers outside Georgia ran a one-sentence condensed telegram among other crimes and casualties.

conflicts.note: The Thomas County headline sits over a Bartow dateline; the local Louisville paper and the wire both say Jefferson County.
